Errors: the claim is another instance's ("is not this fleet's claim"); the worktree shows work, or there is no worktree on this host to show there is none ("is not closed as needing no change"). Nothing was changed.

##### What trips you up

- `--instance` is required, and must be the instance that holds the claim.
- It does not read the verdict. Any claim of the instance whose committed tree equals the base branch's current tree on the remote and has nothing uncommitted is closed, whatever commits the branch holds — one whose worker has only just started as well. A refusal names the differing files.

##### Which checkout it is about

Name it with `-C <CHECKOUT>`: a checkout of the repo, or any directory in one, which names that checkout. What follows the command is its own: the checkout is not among it. Naming none, it is about the checkout it is run in. A worker's worktree is refused as its checkout: only a worker's own commands, and those that only read, are run there.

##### What it logs

As it acts it appends one line to the tick log of this host for this repo, then wakes this host's fleet instance of this repo, through the host runner; its answer says whether it woke one, as "woke": [`afkconvoy help tick-log`](help:tick-log).

#### `afkconvoy escalate`

Hand one of my claims to a human

##### When to run it

To hand a claim to a human by hand. A tick does this on its own for every failure: an `escalate` verdict, a worker silent past its nudge, a blocker that cannot be parked on. Do it yourself when you can see a claim will not finish and the fleet has not given it up yet.

##### Who runs it

The operator, in a checkout of the repo.

##### What it reads and writes

On GitHub it comments `--reason` on the issue, swaps the config's `ready_label` for its `escalate_label`, and writes the status board's last word. In a bound repo it swaps the issue's flow label for the `escalate_label` of the team instead, and the comment records which workflow the issue left: `afkconvoy rule` puts that label back. On the remote it releases the claim. The PR and the branch are kept. The worktree is removed when its tree is clean and every commit of its branch is on the remote — pushed, or on the base branch: a later dispatch recreates it at the pushed tip. Otherwise it is kept, and the comment and the status board say what it holds that exists on this host only, the comment listing each commit the remote does not have by its subject. In orca it closes the terminal of the issue's worker: a worktree that is kept has no worker left in it.

##### What it answers

{"issue", "action": "escalated", "released": true, "worktree", "kept_because", "unpushed"} — worktree is "removed", "kept", or "none" when the issue has none on this host. A kept one says why: kept_because is "dirty", "unpushed" or "unread", and unpushed is how many commits only it holds (null when unread).

{"issue", "released": true, "detail"} — no claim is held on the issue: nothing was done.

Errors: the claim is another instance's ("is not this fleet's claim").

##### What trips you up

- `--instance` is required, and must be the instance that holds the claim.
- It escalates only a claim. On an issue nobody holds it answers `released` with a `detail`, and has neither commented nor relabelled.
- Cut short, run it again with the same reason: it goes on from the step it stopped at, and still posts one comment.
- It stops no worker: one still at work goes on, on an issue the fleet gave up.

##### Which checkout it is about

Name it with `-C <CHECKOUT>`: a checkout of the repo, or any directory in one, which names that checkout. What follows the command is its own: the checkout is not among it. Naming none, it is about the checkout it is run in. A worker's worktree is refused as its checkout: only a worker's own commands, and those that only read, are run there.

##### What it logs

As it acts it appends one line to the tick log of this host for this repo, then wakes this host's fleet instance of this repo, through the host runner; its answer says whether it woke one, as "woke": [`afkconvoy help tick-log`](help:tick-log).

#### `afkconvoy park`

Leave one of my claims waiting on the issues its worker declared it blocked by

##### When to run it

To park a claim by hand. A tick does this on its own for a worker that stopped with a `blocked` verdict naming open issues the fleet can wait for. Do it yourself when a plan keeps showing such a claim under `mine` as `no_pr`.

##### Who runs it

The operator, in a checkout of the repo.

##### What it reads and writes

It reads the worker's latest verdict on the issue and where each issue it names stands. On GitHub it records each blocker as a blocked-by edge of the issue and writes the status board's last word. On the remote it releases the claim. Then the worktree: when its tree is clean and every commit of its branch is on the remote — pushed, or on the base branch — it is removed, and a later dispatch recreates it at the pushed tip. Otherwise it is kept, with the terminal of the issue's worker closed, and the status board says what it holds that exists on this host only.

##### What it answers

{"issue", "action": "parked", "blocked_by", "released": true, "worktree", "kept_because", "unpushed"} — blocked_by is the issues it waits on; worktree is "removed", "kept", or "none" when the issue has none on this host. A kept one says why: kept_because is "dirty" (something uncommitted), "unpushed" (commits the remote does not have) or "unread" (its commits could not be checked against the remote), and unpushed is how many commits only it holds (null when unread).

{"issue", "released": true, "detail"} — no claim is held on the issue: nothing was done.

Errors, each with nothing changed: the claim is another instance's; "is not parkable" — the latest verdict is not `blocked`, or every blocker it named is closed (dispatch the issue again instead), or a blocker cannot be waited for (escalate it instead: the error says why).

##### What trips you up

- `--instance` is required, and must be the instance that holds the claim.
- It takes no blockers of yours: they are the ones the worker's verdict names.

##### Which checkout it is about

Name it with `-C <CHECKOUT>`: a checkout of the repo, or any directory in one, which names that checkout. What follows the command is its own: the checkout is not among it. Naming none, it is about the checkout it is run in. A worker's worktree is refused as its checkout: only a worker's own commands, and those that only read, are run there.

##### What it logs

As it acts it appends one line to the tick log of this host for this repo, then wakes this host's fleet instance of this repo, through the host runner; its answer says whether it woke one, as "woke": [`afkconvoy help tick-log`](help:tick-log).

#### `afkconvoy nudge`

Tell the worker of one of my claims, stopped with no PR and no verdict, to carry on

##### When to run it

To send a worker its nudge by hand. A tick does this on its own, once, for a worker that stopped with no PR and no verdict and stayed quiet for the grace period. Do it yourself when a tick is not running and such a worker sits idle.

##### What counts as silent

A worker is silent when it stopped, declared nothing, showed no sign of life — its terminal's output, a commit, a file touched, being started or nudged — for the grace period (300s), and waits on no background work of its own. Silent, it is nudged once; silent a grace period past that nudge, it is escalated (a joining worker is restarted first, a train worker's train abandoned).

A worker whose turn ended while a shell or a monitor it started in the background still runs — its gate, say — is waiting, not silent: its harness shows that work in the footer under its prompt (Claude Code's `1 shell, 1 monitor`), which the tick reads off its screen, and the tick's line says `waiting on its own background work #7 (since …)`. It is neither nudged nor escalated while it waits. Once that work ends, its silence is counted as ever: a nudge, then escalated past it. Waiting longer than the gate limit (`gate_seconds`) is a silence at once, nudged or not, and the escalation says it waited on its own background work past the limit.

##### Who runs it

The operator, in a checkout of the repo, on the host the worker runs on.

##### What it reads and writes

It asks orca for the worker's state and reads the issue's comments for a verdict. It types one line at the worker's terminal and records the nudge in the worktree. Nothing on GitHub or the remote changes.

##### What it answers

{"issue", "action": "nudged", "terminal"}

Errors, each with nothing sent: "has no stopped worker" — the instance holds no claim on the issue, or its worker is at work or gone; "is not nudged" — it was nudged already, showed a sign of life within the grace period, waits on background work of its own, or declared a verdict; the claim is another instance's; the worktree has no live terminal.

##### What trips you up

- `--instance` is required, and must be the instance that holds the claim.
- It is refused wherever a tick would not nudge: it cannot be used to hurry a worker.
- One nudge per worker. A worker silent again after it is escalated by the next tick.

##### Which checkout it is about

Name it with `-C <CHECKOUT>`: a checkout of the repo, or any directory in one, which names that checkout. What follows the command is its own: the checkout is not among it. Naming none, it is about the checkout it is run in. A worker's worktree is refused as its checkout: only a worker's own commands, and those that only read, are run there.

##### What it logs

As it acts it appends one line to the tick log of this host for this repo, then wakes this host's fleet instance of this repo, through the host runner; its answer says whether it woke one, as "woke": [`afkconvoy help tick-log`](help:tick-log).

#### `afkconvoy restart`

Replace the silent worker of one of my claims whose PR is joining the train, once

##### When to run it

To replace a silent worker by hand. A tick does this on its own, once, for a claim whose PR is open and not on the landing train, and whose worker stopped, was nudged, and stayed silent. Do it yourself when a plan keeps showing such a claim under `mine` as `joining`.

##### Who runs it

The operator, in a checkout of the repo, on the host the worker runs on.

##### What it reads and writes

It records the restart in the fleet's comment on the PR, then starts a new worker in the same worktree, briefed only to join the landing train — in a bound repo, in the landing role of the issue's workflow. The PR, the branch and the worktree are untouched.

##### What it answers

{"issue", "pr", "action": "restarted", "restarted", "terminal", "prompt"} — restarted is the time, in epoch seconds; prompt is the brief the new worker got.

Errors, each with nothing changed: "has no stopped worker" — the instance holds no claim on the issue, its worker is at work or gone, or the issue has no open PR; "is not restarted" — the PR's join already had its restart, the worker was not nudged yet, or it showed a sign of life within the grace period; the claim is another instance's.

##### What trips you up

- `--instance` is required, and must be the instance that holds the claim.
- One restart per PR. A worker silent again after it is escalated by the next tick.
- It is not `dispatch`: for a claim with no PR, continue it with `dispatch`.

##### Which checkout it is about

Name it with `-C <CHECKOUT>`: a checkout of the repo, or any directory in one, which names that checkout. What follows the command is its own: the checkout is not among it. Naming none, it is about the checkout it is run in. A worker's worktree is refused as its checkout: only a worker's own commands, and those that only read, are run there.

##### What it logs

As it acts it appends one line to the tick log of this host for this repo, then wakes this host's fleet instance of this repo, through the host runner; its answer says whether it woke one, as "woke": [`afkconvoy help tick-log`](help:tick-log).

#### `afkconvoy abandon`

Give up the landing train, its worker silent past a nudge, with nothing landed

##### When to run it

To give the landing train up by hand. A tick does this on its own when the train's worker stopped with the train not landed, was nudged, and stayed silent for a grace period more. Do it yourself when a tick is not running and the train stands still.

##### Who runs it

The operator, in a checkout of the repo, on the host the train worker runs on.

##### What it reads and writes

On the remote it deletes the landing train — only while its tip is still the one its worker went silent on. It clears the train's worktree and keeps it. For each PR of the instance that was on the train it records the abandonment in the fleet's comment on the PR and tells the PR's worker — in a bound repo, the one in its workflow's landing role — to join the next train; a PR taken off an abandoned train before is escalated instead. Nothing has landed, and what an earlier train put on the base branch is not touched.

##### What it answers

{"action": "abandoned", "train", "issues", "escalated", "worktree"}

- `train`: the tip of the train given up
- `issues`: the issues whose PRs are to join the next train
- `escalated`: the issues escalated instead
- `worktree`: the train's worktree, kept

Errors, each with nothing abandoned: "nothing is on the landing train"; "has no worktree on this host"; "is not abandoned" — its worker is at work, gone, not told of what the train holds now, not nudged yet, or showed a sign of life within the grace period; "moved while it was being abandoned" — a PR joined meanwhile, and the train was kept.

##### What trips you up

- `--instance` is required. Only that instance's PRs are told to join again.
- It is refused wherever a tick would not abandon: it cannot be used to clear a train whose worker is still at it.
- It takes no `--issue`: a repo has one landing train.

##### Which checkout it is about

Name it after the command, as `[CHECKOUT]`: a checkout of the repo, or any directory in one, which names that checkout. Naming none, it is about the checkout it is run in. A worker's worktree is refused as its checkout: only a worker's own commands, and those that only read, are run there.

##### What it logs

As it acts it appends one line to the tick log of this host for this repo, then wakes this host's fleet instance of this repo, through the host runner; its answer says whether it woke one, as "woke": [`afkconvoy help tick-log`](help:tick-log).

### The claim plumbing

#### `afkconvoy scan`

List every claim and heartbeat on the remote

##### When to run it

To see exactly what the remote holds: which instance claims which issue, and when each instance last beat. `plan` and `takeover --list` say what that means; this is the refs themselves, for repairing them.

##### Who runs it

The operator, in a checkout of the repo.

##### What it reads and writes

It reads the fleet's refs on the remote. It changes nothing, and does not read GitHub or the config.

##### What it answers

{"claims", "heartbeats"}

- `claims`: one per claimed issue, lowest number first: {number, instance, host, ts, sha}. ts is when it was stamped, in epoch seconds; sha is what a take or a release of it is leased to
- `heartbeats`: {<instance id>: <epoch seconds>}

Errors: the remote cannot be read; "is not in a git checkout".

##### What trips you up

- It looks where this repo's last startup probe found the remote keeps the fleet's refs. In a clone no `plan`, `tick` or `run` was ever run in, it looks under refs/convoy/ — and finds nothing on a remote that keeps them as convoy-* branches.
- It does not say whether a claim is live: compare its instance's heartbeat with the lease, or read `takeover --list`.

##### Which checkout it is about

Name it after the command, as `[CHECKOUT]`: a checkout of the repo, or any directory in one, which names that checkout. Naming none, it is about the checkout it is run in. It only reads: a worker's worktree is one too.

#### `afkconvoy claim`

Claim one issue for a fleet instance

##### When to run it

Hardly ever: `dispatch` claims the issue it starts a worker on. Run it to hold an issue back from every fleet — a claim keeps the issue off the frontier — or to repair a claim that was released by mistake.

##### Who runs it

The operator, in a checkout of the repo.

##### What it reads and writes

It creates the issue's claim on the remote in one atomic push, which succeeds for exactly one instance. Before it, it refreshes the instance's heartbeat when that is due. It does not read GitHub: the issue is not checked, and no worker is started.

##### What it answers

{"won": true, "issue", "ref", "sha", "instance"} {"won": false, "issue", "ref", "owner", "detail"} — the issue is claimed already. owner is that claim: {number, instance, host, ts, sha}.

Errors: the push failed and it was not a lost race; the remote cannot be read.

##### What trips you up

- `--instance` is required. A lost race is an answer with exit 0: read `won`.
- A claim the instance holds already answers `won: false`, with itself as the owner.
- A claim is live only while its instance's heartbeat is within the lease. Under an id nothing beats for, another fleet takes it as stale once the lease runs out.
- Claimed as a running fleet's instance, it is a claim with no worker: that fleet's next tick starts a worker on it.

##### Which checkout it is about

Name it with `-C <CHECKOUT>`: a checkout of the repo, or any directory in one, which names that checkout. What follows the command is its own: the checkout is not among it. Naming none, it is about the checkout it is run in. A worker's worktree is refused as its checkout: only a worker's own commands, and those that only read, are run there.

##### What it logs

As it acts it appends one line to the tick log of this host for this repo, then wakes this host's fleet instance of this repo, through the host runner; its answer says whether it woke one, as "woke": [`afkconvoy help tick-log`](help:tick-log).

#### `afkconvoy release`

Release a fleet instance's own claim on one issue

##### When to run it

Hardly ever: `close`, `escalate` and `park` release the claim they end, and a landed PR's claim is released by the tick. Run it to drop a claim made with `claim`, or one left behind by something that went wrong.

##### Who runs it

The operator, in a checkout of the repo.

##### What it reads and writes

It deletes the issue's claim on the remote, only while it is still the claim that was read. It does not read or change GitHub, and touches no worker and no worktree.

##### What it answers

{"released": true, "issue", "ref"} — also when the issue had no claim: already gone counts as released.

Errors: the claim is another instance's ("is not this fleet's claim"); it "moved since it was read" — somebody took it meanwhile, and it was left alone; the delete failed.

##### What trips you up

- `--instance` is required, and must be the instance that holds the claim. To end another instance's claim, take it first: `takeover`.
- It only unlocks. The issue keeps its labels, its worker keeps working, and — still open and ready — the issue is back on the frontier: a fleet dispatches it again.

##### Which checkout it is about

Name it with `-C <CHECKOUT>`: a checkout of the repo, or any directory in one, which names that checkout. What follows the command is its own: the checkout is not among it. Naming none, it is about the checkout it is run in. A worker's worktree is refused as its checkout: only a worker's own commands, and those that only read, are run there.

##### What it logs

As it acts it appends one line to the tick log of this host for this repo, then wakes this host's fleet instance of this repo, through the host runner; its answer says whether it woke one, as "woke": [`afkconvoy help tick-log`](help:tick-log).

#### `afkconvoy heartbeat`

Refresh a fleet instance's heartbeat, if it is due

##### When to run it

Hardly ever: every tick refreshes its instance's heartbeat. Run it to keep the claims of an instance live while nothing ticks for it — claims made by hand, or a fleet stopped for a while whose claims no other host should take.

##### Who runs it

The operator, in a checkout of the repo.

##### What it reads and writes

It reads the instance's heartbeat on the remote and, when it is due — never written, or older than a third of the lease — writes it anew. Nothing on GitHub changes.

##### What it answers

{"refreshed": true, "ts", "ref"} {"refreshed": false, "reason": "not due", "ts", "ref"} — ts is the heartbeat that stands, in epoch seconds.

Errors: the remote cannot be read, or refuses the push.

##### What trips you up

- `--instance` is required.
- It keeps a dead fleet's claims alive: while they are beaten for, no other host takes them as stale, and nobody works them.
- One beat lasts one lease. Kept up by hand, it has to be run again before that.

##### Which checkout it is about

Name it after the command, as `[CHECKOUT]`: a checkout of the repo, or any directory in one, which names that checkout. Naming none, it is about the checkout it is run in. A worker's worktree is refused as its checkout: only a worker's own commands, and those that only read, are run there.

##### What it logs

As it acts it appends one line to the tick log of this host for this repo, then wakes this host's fleet instance of this repo, through the host runner; its answer says whether it woke one, as "woke": [`afkconvoy help tick-log`](help:tick-log).

### Run by a human an issue waits for

#### `afkconvoy rule`

Answer an escalated issue with a ruling: its stage runs again under it (a human's command, and a consult's for the stage that asked it)

##### When to run it

When an issue of a bound repo was escalated and you have decided what it asked: the issue carries the team's escalate label in place of its flow label, and the comment above the label says why. Answer it with the ruling:

```
afkconvoy rule 7 --text "Keep the v1 schema; migrate in a later issue."
```

The issue's number is an argument, or `--issue 7`: one of the two. The comment of the escalation ends with this line, the number filled in, and `afkconvoy doctor` lists it for every issue that waits (`waiting_on_human`).

The stage the issue stopped at runs again under the ruling, and both rework counts start over from it. `afkconvoy show --issue 7` says which stage that is before you rule. To put the issue at another stage instead, see `afkconvoy send --help`.

Or as a consult: the issue was at a stage that names one (`escalate: { to, do }` in its workflow), and would have gone to a human — the stage declared `escalate`, a breaker tripped, it failed, or its workflow changed — so the fleet started you in that role to answer it first. The stage comes from your environment:

```
afkconvoy rule --issue 7 --text-file /tmp/ruling.md
```

The stage runs again under your ruling. What is not yours to rule on you let through to a human instead, with `afkconvoy verdict escalate` — your brief gives that line too.

##### Who runs it

The operator, or whichever human the issue was handed to: in a checkout of the bound repo, with no commit named and none in the environment.

Or a consult, in the issue's worktree: the fleet put the commits of its role and of its team in its environment, and those are what make the ruling a consult's; the harness it is a session of is there too, and its record names it. No other worker runs it: a stage does not rule on itself.

##### What it reads and writes

It reads the team the config names, the claims on the remote, and the issue's labels and comments. The workflow is the one the issue's flow label names; with the label swapped out, the one its escalation's comment says it left.

It writes one comment on the issue — a stage record that carries the ruling, says a human left it and names the stage — then puts the flow label back on and takes the team's `escalate_label` off, and wakes the fleet. The record is written first: once the flow label is back the issue is the fleet's again, and its next tick starts a worker on the stage, with the ruling in its brief.

A consult's ruling is one comment too, and nothing else: a stage record that says the stage's consult left it, under the claim the consult holds on the issue, with the two commits. `--stage` is AFKCONVOY_STAGE where not given. It moves no label — the issue never left the fleet — and the next tick ends the consult's claim; the one after starts the stage that asked, with the ruling in its brief. It is checked no more than a worker's verdict is.

The ruling is `--text`, or the contents of `--text-file`: one of the two, not empty.

##### What it answers

{"issue", "workflow", "stage", "ruled": true, "relabelled", "woke"} {"issue", "stage", "verdict": "ruling", "claim", "declared", "woke"} — a consult's, as `afkconvoy verdict` answers a worker

- `stage`: the stage that runs again under the ruling
- `relabelled`: whether a label was moved; false when the issue already carried its flow label and no escalate label
- `woke`: whether a `run` on this host was told, as `afkconvoy wake` answers

Errors, as {"error": …} with a non-zero exit, with nothing written: the issue "is claimed" — its escalation is still under way, or a worker is at it; it "is not escalated" — its records put it at a stage and it carries its flow label; it "cannot be ruled on" — it has left the stages of its workflow, or no flow label and no escalation says which workflow it follows; no text, or an empty one; the repo names no team; and every error of `afkconvoy check`. A consult's: `--stage` is missing, or given with no commits; the issue "is not claimed".

##### What trips you up

- A ruling runs the same stage again. It does not decide the stage's verdict: the worker started under it does.
- An issue escalated because its worker went silent, or its gate stayed red, is at the stage that worker was performing: a ruling starts that stage anew.
- An escalation made before its comment named the workflow cannot say which flow label to put back. Put the flow label on by hand, then rule.
- Moving the labels by hand hands the issue back with no ruling on record: an issue its records show as escalating is escalated again at the next tick.
- Run twice, it leaves two rulings. Both count: the stage runs again once. A consult's second changes nothing: one claim declares once.
- A human's ruling starts both rework counts over. A consult's does not. On an `escalate` it is one more of the issue's rework in total, and one that would pass `max_rework` goes to a human instead; on anything else it counts nothing, and the same hand-off again goes to a human.
- A consult writes no code. The guard refuses its commits and pushes, and a commit it left on the branch all the same is a failure: the issue escalates, whatever it ruled.

##### Which checkout it is about

Name it with `-C <CHECKOUT>`: a checkout of the repo, or any directory in one, which names that checkout. What follows the command is its own: the checkout is not among it. Naming none, it is about the checkout it is run in. A worker runs it in its own worktree.

##### What it logs

As it acts it appends one line to the tick log of this host for this repo, then wakes this host's fleet instance of this repo, through the host runner; its answer says whether it woke one, as "woke": [`afkconvoy help tick-log`](help:tick-log).

#### `afkconvoy send`

Send an issue to a named stage of its workflow (a human's command, and a consult's)

##### When to run it

To put an issue of a bound repo at a stage of your choosing, whatever its records say: back to planning after a review that missed the point, past a stage you have done by hand, or out of an escalation to another stage than the one that asked.

```
afkconvoy send --issue 7 --stage plan --text "The approach changed: see #12."
```

The issue is then at that stage, to be performed, with both rework counts started over. To answer an escalated issue where it stopped, `afkconvoy rule` is the command.

##### Who runs it

The operator, or whichever human steers the issue: in a checkout of the bound repo. Or a consult answering in a human's place, under its claim, as with `afkconvoy rule`; its send starts no count over. No other worker runs it: where an issue goes is its workflow's to say, or a human's.

##### What it reads and writes

It reads the team the config names, the claims on the remote, and the issue's labels and comments. The workflow is the one the issue's flow label names; for an escalated issue, the one its escalation's comment says it left.

It writes one comment on the issue — a stage record that names the stage, says a human sent the issue there and carries the text — and wakes the fleet. An escalated issue also gets its flow label back and loses the team's `escalate_label`, after the record is written. Nothing else moves: the next tick reads the issue's position off its records, starts a worker on the stage if a role performs it, and waits for a human's verdict if the stage is `by: human`.

The text is `--text`, or the contents of `--text-file`: one of the two, not empty. The worker started on the stage is shown it in its brief.

##### What it answers

{"issue", "workflow", "stage", "sent": true, "relabelled", "woke"}

- `relabelled`: whether a label was moved: true for an issue that was escalated
- `woke`: whether a `run` on this host was told, as `afkconvoy wake` answers

Errors, as {"error": …} with a non-zero exit, with nothing written: the workflow "has no stage" of that name — the error lists the ones it has; the issue "is claimed" — a worker is at a stage of it; it "cannot be sent to a stage" — no flow label and no escalation says which workflow it follows; no text, or an empty one; the repo names no team; and every error of `afkconvoy check`.

##### What trips you up

- It is refused while the issue is claimed: a claim is dispatched to one stage, and its worker would go on performing it. Wait for the stage to declare, or hand the claim to a human with `afkconvoy escalate` first.
- It reopens nothing and closes nothing. An issue sent back from an ended workflow must be open to be worked.
- The stage is named as its workflow's file names it. `afkconvoy show` draws them.
- Run twice, it leaves two records; the issue is at the stage either way.

##### Which checkout it is about

Name it with `-C <CHECKOUT>`: a checkout of the repo, or any directory in one, which names that checkout. What follows the command is its own: the checkout is not among it. Naming none, it is about the checkout it is run in. A worker runs it in its own worktree.

##### What it logs

As it acts it appends one line to the tick log of this host for this repo, then wakes this host's fleet instance of this repo, through the host runner; its answer says whether it woke one, as "woke": [`afkconvoy help tick-log`](help:tick-log).

## Topics

### `afkconvoy help concepts`

What becomes of one issue, from the moment it is the fleet's to the moment it lands, and the four things that carry it there. Each term has its one definition in [`afkconvoy help glossary`](help:glossary); each paragraph ends with what says more.

## The four things

- **The fleet**: A fleet instance is one `afkconvoy run` on one host, for one repo. It works in ticks: each reads fleet state anew from GitHub and the repo's remote, then does everything that calls for. No process holds fleet state, so a `run` that is killed loses nothing and several hosts can work one repo. `afkconvoy run --help`, `afkconvoy tick --help`.
- **A worker**: A session of one harness — Claude Code, pi or Codex — started for one issue, in a git worktree of that issue's own. It reports through GitHub alone: a PR, a comment. The fleet never waits on one; it reads what the worker left at the next tick. `afkconvoy dispatch --help`.
- **A claim**: What marks one issue as one fleet instance's. Creating it succeeds for exactly one instance, so no issue is worked twice. It is live while its owner's heartbeat is; past that another host may take it. `afkconvoy scan --help`, `afkconvoy takeover --help`.
- **The landing train**: The one line of merge commits ahead of the base branch that finished PRs join, one merge commit each. One worker gates its tip and pushes it to the base branch as a fast-forward: what lands is a tree the gate passed. `afkconvoy land --help`.
- **The gate limit**: How long the gate may run: `gate_seconds` in the repo's config, 3600 where it sets none. A run that reaches it is ended and is red, a worker's and the train's alike. `afkconvoy config --help`.

## One issue, in an unbound repo

An unbound repo's config names no team: every issue takes the same path, with one worker from start to landing. It is where to start when issues turned into PRs is all you want; bind the repo to a team once the work is to be judged by another than the worker that wrote it before it lands.

1. Intake. A human puts the ready label on the issue. It is on the frontier once it is open, unclaimed, under no epic label, with no open blocker and no open PR linked to it but one of the fleet's own that an escalation or a park kept, off the landing train: its worker takes that PR up. `afkconvoy plan` shows the frontier, and why each other issue waits.
2. Dispatch. A tick claims it and starts a worker in a new worktree, on a new branch cut from the base branch, with a prompt that names the issue and every command the worker ends with.
3. The work. The worker changes the code, runs `afkconvoy gate` until the gate is green on what it committed, opens a PR, and joins it to the landing train with `afkconvoy land`. Then it wakes the fleet: `afkconvoy wake`.
4. Landing. The train worker gates the train's tip and pushes it to the base branch. The PR is merged by that push, the issue closes, the claim is released.
5. Or no PR. The worker says so in a comment on the issue instead: there was nothing to change, and the issue closes; it waits on other issues, and is parked until they close; or it cannot go on, and the issue escalates — it is handed to a human, with why. A worker that stops having left nothing is nudged once, and escalated after that. Every failure escalates: [`afkconvoy help humans`](help:humans).
6. Or a red gate that is not its own. A worker that proves its gate red for a defect outside its issue — what its gate merged in is red the same way gated alone — records the defect itself: it comments on the open issue that already records it, or opens one with the ready label, and parks its issue on that one with `blocked`. It is the one `blocked` whose blocker the worker opens. When that issue closes, its own is on the frontier again. The train worker does the same for a base branch that is red without the train, with no issue to park — in a bound repo taking the issue in to a workflow (`afkconvoy intake --train`) in place of the ready label.

## One issue, in a bound repo

A bound repo's config names a team. The issue passes through the stages of one of the team's workflows, and each stage is performed by a new worker, started in the role that stage names.

1. Intake. The issue is given a flow label — `flow:<workflow>`, or the one the workflow's file names with `label`: by a human on GitHub, or by a patrol's worker through `afkconvoy intake`. `afkconvoy flows` says which workflow takes which issue, and creates the labels. An issue with no flow label is left alone.
2. Its position. Each tick derives where the issue is from the stage records on it — comments — and from the workflow. Nothing stores it: the `stage:<name>` label the fleet keeps on the issue is for a human to filter by, and is never read back. `afkconvoy show --issue <n>` says where an issue is, and what led there.
3. A stage. A tick claims the issue and starts a worker in the stage's role, in the issue's worktree, to perform the skill the stage names. The worker ends by declaring a verdict with `afkconvoy verdict`, which leaves the stage record:
   - `pass`: on to where the workflow says: a later stage, the landing, or the end of the workflow
   - `reject`: back to an earlier stage, which runs again: rework. Breakers bound it, and the rework past one escalates
   - `blocked`: parked until the issues it waits on close
   - `already-satisfied`: nothing needs changing: the workflow ends
   - `escalate`: to the stage's consult — a worker in a more senior role, or afkconvoy's stock consult where it names none, who rules or lets it through — or to a human where it says so
4. The next stage. The tick that reads a verdict ends that stage's claim and starts the stage that follows, under a claim of its own, with a new worker: the one that judges a piece of work never inherits the reasoning of the one that wrote it.
5. Landing. Once the last stage passes, a new worker in the workflow's landing role gates the PR and joins it to the landing train. From there it lands as an unbound repo's does.

## What holds all the way

- The gate is the only machine verification between a worker and the base branch: one command of the repo's, which exits 0 only on a good tree. `afkconvoy gate --help`.
- Nothing is ever rebased. A branch is brought up to date by merging into it.
- No human stands in a workflow unless a stage is given to one. A human is asked by exception, and each way that happens has its command: [`afkconvoy help humans`](help:humans).
- Every worker of a bound repo works under the guard, which refuses what no worker may do — merging a PR, pushing the base branch, moving a flow label. `afkconvoy guard --help`.
- A fleet lock — an open issue under the lock label — makes the fleet work lock issues only until it closes: for a fault every issue shares, as a broken base branch is. `afkconvoy lock --help`.

## Where to read on

- [`afkconvoy help roles`](help:roles): what a role is, and how to write a good one
- [`afkconvoy help humans`](help:humans): every way the fleet stops for a human
- [`afkconvoy help troubleshooting`](help:troubleshooting): a symptom, its cause and its fix
- [`afkconvoy help team`](help:team): the files of a team and of a role, key by key

### `afkconvoy help team`

A team is a directory — a whole repo, or a subdirectory of one — that names a set of roles and holds the workflows, patrols and precedents they work by. Read this to write a team, bind a repo to one, or understand a fault from `afkconvoy check`.

## What its directory holds

- `team.md`: the team file
- `CLAUDE.md`: the team rules: what every worker of the team works under
- `workflows/<name>.md`: one file per workflow: [`afkconvoy help workflows`](help:workflows)
- `patrols/<name>.md`: one file per patrol: [`afkconvoy help patrols`](help:patrols)
- `precedents.md`: the precedents: one line per ruling a human accepted

Only each definition file's first `` ```yaml `` block is read; the rest explains it.

## The team file

```yaml
escalate_label: ready-for-human    # default
roles:
  <short name>: <its directory>    # owner/repo, owner/repo/path or ./path
  <short name>: { dir: <its directory>, host_user: false }   # its own host_user
roster:                            # optional: `afkconvoy help roster`
  <short name>: { cast: <how to cast>, run: [{ harness: pi, model: <model>,
    good_at: <what it does best> }] }   # cast, model and good_at optional
precedents: { by: <role>, do: <skill>, max_open: 10 }   # optional
host_user: true                    # default
dsh_profile: fleet                # fleet (default) or host-user; DSH only
split: true                        # default; false omits splitting
```

`escalate_label` is the label an issue handed to a human carries in place of its flow label. `roles` gives each role the short name a `by` or a `to` says. `precedents` names who proposes a human's ruling as a precedent: for each ruling a human gives an escalated issue (`afkconvoy rule`) a worker in the role `by`, with the skill `do`, opens a PR on the team's repo that appends one entry to `precedents.md`, unless `max_open` are open; none without the key (`afkconvoy tick --help`). `host_user`, true or false, says whether a worker is given the host user's own skills and rules beside its role's ([`afkconvoy help roles`](help:roles)); a role named by `dir` may set its own. `dsh_profile`: `fleet` (default) or `host-user`; independent of `host_user`. A role's `{ dir, dsh_profile }` says its own. Details: `afkconvoy run --help`. `split: false` omits splitting from briefs; true or unsaid offers it, with no guard.

## How it names a role

A role is a directory too, and the team file names it in one of three ways:

- `owner/repo`: a whole repo
- `owner/repo/path`: a subdirectory of a repo: the first two segments are the repo, the rest the path from its root
- `./path`: a subdirectory of the repo the team itself is in

A `./path` is read from the root of the team's repo, not from the team's directory: a team and its roles in one repo name no repo at all, and two teams of one repo name the same role alike. Every role is read at the head of its repo's default branch, and nothing names a branch or a tag. A role's directory is not the team's and does not contain it, is not inside the team's `workflows/` or `patrols/`, and neither contains another role's nor is inside one. It holds:

- `CLAUDE.md`: its rules: what a worker in it always works under
- `.claude/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md`: one directory per skill it can be asked for
- `.claude/settings.json`: its limits for claude-code: hooks, and the permissions it denies
- `.pi/extensions/`: its limits for pi: extensions
- `.codex/hooks.json`: its limits for codex: hooks
- `.dsh/cordis.patch.yml`: its limits for dsh: a DSH overlay

Only a skill's file has keys `check` reads: [`afkconvoy help skill-file`](help:skill-file). A `do` names an entry of `.claude/skills/` in the role. Rules and skills are written once; limits per harness, in its own form (`afkconvoy run --help` says how each loads a role).

A worker is given its role's directory alone, and nothing else of its repo: a `CLAUDE.md` or a `.claude/` in a directory above the role is loaded for a session opened there by hand, and a worker never sees it — and a symlink that leaves the role's directory would point at nothing. The team's directory is given to every worker beside its role's, without the directories of its roles and without a `.claude/` at its top: a worker's skills and hooks are its role's.

## The team rules

The `CLAUDE.md` in the team's directory, and optional. Every worker of the team is given it, whatever its role and whatever it was started for — a stage, a consult, a patrol, the proposal of a precedent, a landing — and no key turns it off. A role two teams name works under the rules of the team whose stage it is in.

They are one of four kinds of text a worker reads, beside the repo's own rules, its role's rules and the precedents; the host user's rules give way to all four. Whose:

- **its role's**: the CLAUDE.md of the role's directory, under every harness
- **the team rules**: the CLAUDE.md of the team's directory, under every harness
- **the repo's own**: of the repo an issue is of: under claude-code its CLAUDE.md; under pi and codex its AGENTS.md, or CLAUDE.md where it has none

Claude Code and pi load the three; the fleet names the other two to Codex. What each is for, and where a sentence belongs: [`afkconvoy help roles`](help:roles).

## How a repo is bound to it

By its config, on its base branch (`afkconvoy config --help` shows the file whole):

- `team`: owner/repo or owner/repo/path: naming it is what binds the repo
- `patrols`: which of the team's patrols run here, by name; none by default
- `intake_limit`: the open issues taken in by workers, at most; 50 by default

The team is read at the head of its repo's default branch: pushing is the only way an edit reaches a worker. An issue of a bound repo is the fleet's to work only while it carries a flow label, which `afkconvoy flows` creates: [`afkconvoy help workflows`](help:workflows).

## What `check` holds it to

`afkconvoy check` loads a team and answers every fault at once, each with its file and key; `afkconvoy check --help` lists them all. Those a role's directory can hold:

- A role's directory that holds an `AGENTS.md`, an `AGENTS.MD` or an `AGENTS.override.md` is a fault: pi and Codex load one in place of `CLAUDE.md`.
- A role that holds limits for one harness and none for another is right for the first alone: a roster entry that lets it run the other is a fault. One with no limits is right for every harness; two that refuse alike are the role's to see to.
- A `.claude/` in the team's directory is no fault and is loaded by no worker: a note.

## Where to read on

- [`afkconvoy help roles`](help:roles): what goes where in a role, and what makes one good
- [`afkconvoy help roster`](help:roster): what each role's workers may run, and an issue's casting
- [`afkconvoy help workflows`](help:workflows): the stages an issue passes through, and every key of them
- [`afkconvoy help patrols`](help:patrols): a role run on a schedule, intake and the fleet lock
- [`afkconvoy help glossary`](help:glossary): each term used here, with its one definition

### `afkconvoy help roles`

What a role is, what goes where in one, and what makes one good. The files of a role, path by path and harness by harness, are in [`afkconvoy help team`](help:team); a skeleton of one is written by `afkconvoy scaffold role`. What a skill's file holds — its path, its frontmatter, its keys — is in [`afkconvoy help skill-file`](help:skill-file).

## What a role is

A role is a directory that defines one kind of worker. A worker of a bound repo is a session of its harness started in that directory, with the issue's worktree beside it: open the directory by hand and you are in the role a worker is in. Of your own configuration it loads your skills and rules alone (below). The directory holds three things:

- **its rules**: what a worker in it always works under, whatever it is asked
- **its skills**: each one thing it can be asked to perform; a stage's `do` names one ([`afkconvoy help skill-file`](help:skill-file))
- **its limits**: what it may never do, in the form its harness enforces: hooks for Claude Code and for Codex, extensions for pi

A role names no workflow and no stage. The workflow says in which order the work is done and who judges whom; a role serves as many workflows as name it.

A change to a role reaches a worker only once it is pushed to the default branch of the role's repo: a stage starts under what is at the head when it starts.

## What goes where

- **a rule the role follows whatever it is asked**: its rules: they are loaded for every stage the role performs
- **how to perform one kind of work**: a skill: a stage's `do` names it
- **something the role must never do**: a limit: a sentence can be ignored; a hook refuses
- **the order of the work, and who judges whom**: the workflow: a role serves many workflows and names none
- **what must hold before any change lands**: the repo's gate: a role's limits do not see the repo's code
- **what one codebase asks of whoever changes it**: the repo's own rules: they are loaded from the worktree, in every role
- **how the team works, in every repo bound to it**: the team rules: every worker of the team is given them

## Why a limit is a hook and not a sentence

A worker reads its rules and still does, now and then, what they forbid: a rule is text a model weighs against the task in front of it. A hook is not weighed. The harness runs it before each thing the worker does, and when it refuses, the thing is not done and the worker is shown why. It holds although a worker runs with every permission prompt bypassed, since nobody is at its terminal to be asked.

So write as a sentence what you want done well, and as a limit what must not happen at all: a commit made past its hooks, a branch rebased, a test deleted. The fleet adds a limit of its own to every worker of a bound repo — the guard, for what no worker of any role may do (`afkconvoy guard --help`); a role's limits add what that role may not. Either stops a worker that errs, not one that sets out to get past it: the gate still stands between every change and the base branch.

## The four kinds of text a worker reads

A worker of a bound repo works under four kinds of text. Each is for one thing, and a sentence belongs in exactly one of them:

- **the repo's own rules**: what one codebase asks: how it is built and tested, what its conventions are. True for every role that touches it, and for no other repo.
- **the team rules**: how the team works: what every role holds to, in every repo bound to the team. True whatever the codebase.
- **the role's rules**: what one kind of worker does and does not do, whichever stage it is in and whichever repo it is in.
- **the precedents**: what a human ruled before, on a question a stage could not decide: followed instead of asking again.

To place a sentence, ask whom it would still be true for. For this codebase under any team: the repo's own rules. For this team in any codebase: the team rules. For this kind of worker alone: its role's. And if nobody could have written it down before the question came up, it is a ruling, and becomes a precedent when a human accepts it ([`afkconvoy help humans`](help:humans)). The four have no order: two that contradict each other are a defect of the files, and nothing says which holds.

## The host user's skills and rules

A worker is also given the skills and the rules of the host's own user, as a session that user opens by hand has them — Claude Code's ~/.claude/skills and CLAUDE.md, pi's and Codex's in ~/.pi/agent and ~/.codex — so a role need not copy in the skills its author relies on everywhere. Except for DSH's explicit `dsh_profile: host-user` choice ([`afkconvoy help team`](help:team)), never their settings, hooks, MCP servers or extensions: the guard and orca's report stay the only hooks the fleet adds. A role's skill wins over one of theirs of the same name, and the brief, the role's rules, the team rules and the repo's own rules win over theirs; the brief says so. The cost: a role may behave differently on two hosts. A team file that says `host_user: false` gives its workers none of it, and every role is what its directory says on every host. One role may say it for itself, whatever the team says — `reviewer: { dir: ./roles/reviewer, host_user: false }` — and its workers alone are given none of it, on every harness; the team's other roles keep the team's ([`afkconvoy help team`](help:team)).

## What makes a role good

- It names no stage and no workflow. The brief the fleet writes for each worker carries the issue, the stage, the worktree, the stage records so far and the exact commands to end with. A skill that says "end as your brief says" stays right when the workflow changes.
- Its skills say how; the brief says what. The brief is a fixed form with nothing of how to do the work well. What a plan contains, what a judge looks for, what is looked at before a landing: that is the skill's to say.
- The one who writes and the one who judges are different roles, and every judging stage is `writes: false`. A judge that can fix what it finds stops reporting it.
- `reject` has a bar. A judge with no rule about when to reject sends work back over a name. Say what blocks and what is a note, and that notes alone are a `pass`. The breakers end a loop; a bar keeps it from starting.
- It says what is not its to decide. The most useful sentence in a role is the one that tells it when to stop and declare `escalate`. Without it a worker decides what a user of the code will see, and you learn of it in the diff.
- It is taught the three verdicts no workflow writes — `blocked`, `already-satisfied` and `escalate` — once, in its rules: they mean the same at every stage.
- It is small. One role and one stage that lands is a working team; add the judge once you have read what the first role produces. `afkconvoy rehearse` tries a workflow out with no worker started, and `afkconvoy check` holds every edit to what the fleet will accept.

### `afkconvoy help roster`

A team's roster says what each of its roles' workers may run: which harnesses, on which models, in what order. Read this to write one, to see why a worker started on the harness it did, or to see why a role's stages wait.

## The roster

The `roster` of the team file ([`afkconvoy help team`](help:team)) holds an entry per role it names, by the role's short name:

```yaml
roster:
  dev:
    cast: Hard or wide work on fable; the rest on opus.   # optional
    run:                           # one at least, in order of preference
      - { harness: claude-code, model: opus, good_at: most work }
      - { harness: claude-code, model: fable, good_at: hard or wide work }
      - { harness: pi }            # any model the host kit holds for pi
  reviewer:
    run: [{ harness: codex, model: gpt-5.5 }]
```

Each of `run` names a `harness` — claude-code, pi, codex or dsh — and may name a `model` by any of its names on that harness — its id, as the host kit holds it and `afkconvoy draft` writes it, or another name it answered to, whatever the case, the provider prefix left off where that leaves one match (`afkconvoy kit --help`) — and `good_at`, what it is good at, which the caster is told. `afkconvoy draft` copies good_at from the host kit's sourced, one-time research; its model supplies only the role's cast guidance. No human edits the host kit to supply it. One that names no model allows any model the host kit holds for the harness, or the harness's command as written where the host kit holds none. `cast` says, in the team's words, how an issue is to be cast among them: the caster is told it too. A role the roster names no entry for may run whatever the host kit holds, but a harness it holds no limits for (below). A model an entry names that matches none the host kit holds for its harness is cut from the range: `check`, `plan` and `doctor` name the entry, what the host kit holds and the nearest names, and a tick opens one issue for it in the team's repo, with that repo's ready label, for the team's own fleet to correct — none while one for it is open. The fleet never changes a roster.

A roster is drafted rather than written from nothing: `afkconvoy draft`, in a checkout of the team, writes one into team.md from this host's host kit — every role, every harness and model in the host kit's order, what the host kit's first model says each is good at and how to cast — and commits nothing. A human reads it, edits it and commits it; the fleet never changes a team's roster.

## A role's range

On a host, a role's range is its entry cut to the host kit (`afkconvoy kit --help`), in the roster's order: a harness, or a model, the host kit does not hold is left out. An entry the host kit holds nothing of is not followed: the role ranges over the host kit whole, as if the roster named none for it, and `check`, `plan` and `doctor` name the entry. So is a harness the role holds no limits for while it holds limits for another: no worker of the role runs a harness it holds no limits for, and a host kit may hold every harness its host can start. `afkconvoy check` and `afkconvoy plan` name each harness a range leaves out, and why (`no limits for pi`). `afkconvoy check` answers each role's entry and its range on the host it runs on; `afkconvoy show` draws the roster under the workflows.

## An issue's casting

An issue's casting is its `harness:` and `model:` labels, which the caster (`afkconvoy cast --help`) or a human puts on — the model by any of its names, a caster’s by its id; the caster is given each stage's range, and casts only an issue some range leaves a choice in. A worker for an issue — its stage's, its consult's, its landing's — runs the casting when its role's range holds it, the range's first when it does not or the issue has none, and the range's one where it holds one harness and one model, whatever the casting. `afkconvoy plan` says which, and why. A name that matches nothing never stops work: a casting no range of the issue's workflow's stages holds runs each stage's range's first, `plan` says `unmatched` and names the label, and the issue is told once, in a comment, what ran instead and what the host kit holds. The label stays, and is followed again once the host kit holds it. A patrol's worker, which has no issue, runs its role's range's first. A harness `afkconvoy switch` chose on a host runs every worker there, whatever the roster and the casting say; one the host kit does not hold is not followed, and each worker runs its range's first, `unmatched`.

## What is refused, and what only waits

- A stage, a patrol and a config name no harness and no model: `check` refuses one that does, with the line to delete and the roster entry to write in its place.
- In the roster, `check` refuses an entry for a name that is no role, a `run` that is missing or empty, a harness that is none, an allowance written twice, and a harness the role holds no limits for while it holds limits for another.
- Nothing about a range refuses a start. A role whose range on a host is empty — it holds limits for no harness the host kit holds, paused harnesses left out — has no worker started without its limits: its stages wait, `plan` says why on each issue at one, and `doctor` and the panel name the role, while every other stage goes on. They go on by themselves once the host kit holds a harness it holds limits for: add one with `afkconvoy kit`, or write the role's limits for one the host kit holds.

## Where to read on

- [`afkconvoy help team`](help:team): the team file the roster is a key of
- `afkconvoy draft --help`: a roster drafted from the host kit
- `afkconvoy kit --help`: what this host can start, and on which models
- `afkconvoy cast --help`: the caster, and the labels it puts on
- [`afkconvoy help glossary`](help:glossary): each term used here, with its one definition

### `afkconvoy help skill-file`

What a skill's file holds: where it is, what it opens with, and what `afkconvoy check` holds it to. What belongs in a skill and what in a role's rules or its limits is in [`afkconvoy help roles`](help:roles); the other files of a role are in [`afkconvoy help team`](help:team).

## Where it is

A skill is a directory of its role's `.claude/skills/`, and its file is the `SKILL.md` there. The directory's name is the skill's: it is what a `do` says — a stage's, a consult's, a landing's, a patrol's — and what the file's `name` says. A role with the skills `review` and `rule` holds:

```text
.claude/skills/review/SKILL.md
.claude/skills/rule/SKILL.md
```

The skills are written once, there, whatever harness a stage runs the role on.

## What it holds

```markdown
---
name: review
description: Review the code an issue's PR holds, and pass or reject it. Use
  when the brief you were started with names `review` as the skill to perform.
---

# review

1. Read the issue, every comment on it, and the diff of its PR.
2. Reject what blocks; say what is only a note, and pass on notes alone.
3. End as the brief you were started with says to.
```

The file opens with frontmatter: a first line `---`, yaml, and a line `---`. Every harness reads two keys of it, and both must be there:

- `name`: the skill's name: the name of its directory, letter for letter
- `description`: what the skill does and when to use it, in a sentence or two. A harness shows a worker this and not the file, until the worker loads the skill: say there that the brief names it

Any other key is one harness's own, and the fleet reads none. What stands under the frontmatter is the skill: markdown, in whatever form says how the work is done well. Other files of the directory are the skill's to name and a worker's to open.

## What `check` holds it to

`afkconvoy check` reads the `SKILL.md` of every skill a `do` names, and a fault at that `do` is one of:

- the skill's directory holds no `SKILL.md`
- the file does not open with frontmatter, or its yaml cannot be read
- its `name` is missing, or is not the name of its directory
- its `description` is missing or empty

A skill no `do` names is not read: a role may hold skills by other authors, which a worker loads when its own skill says to. What the file says under its frontmatter is nobody's to check but yours: [`afkconvoy help roles`](help:roles) says what makes it good.

- [`afkconvoy help roles`](help:roles): what goes in a skill, and what in rules and limits

### `afkconvoy help workflows`

A workflow is the stages one issue passes through and where each verdict leads, ending in the landing train or in nothing more to do. Read this to write a file of a team's `workflows/`, or to tell why an issue went where it did.

## A workflow's file

`workflows/<name>.md` is the workflow `<name>`: an issue that carries its flow label is at the first stage. That is `flow:<name>`, or what `label` names — `ready-for-agent` takes issues opened the usual way; an epic stays out. Above the yaml block, say what the workflow is for and what an issue of it holds: `afkconvoy flows` answers that prose to whoever opens an issue, and `afkconvoy check` warns of a file that says nothing there.

```yaml
label: <label>                     # optional; default flow:<name>
max_rework: 3                      # default
max_consecutive_rework: 2          # default
stages:
  - name: <unique; not land, done or human>
    by: <role> | human
    do: <skill>                    # required unless by: human
    writes: false                  # optional; default true
    escalate: { to: <role>, do: <skill> } | { to: human }  # optional: the consult
    on: { pass: <stage> | land | done, reject: <earlier stage> }   # reject optional
land: { by: <role>, do: <skill> }  # required exactly when a pass leads to land
```

## Stages

A stage is one skill of one role, performed by one new worker: `by` is a short name of the team file, `do` an entry of that role's `.claude/skills/`. The worker of a stage knows nothing of the one before it but what the stage records say, so a stage that judges never inherits the reasoning of the one that wrote.

A stage names neither a harness nor a model. What its worker runs is its role's range's to say, picked among by the issue's casting ([`afkconvoy help roster`](help:roster)).

`writes: false` has the guard refuse the stage's worker a commit and a push: mark every stage that judges so.

## Verdicts, and where each leads

A worker ends its stage with `afkconvoy verdict`, which leaves a stage record on the issue. Where an issue is, is derived from those records each tick and stored nowhere: `afkconvoy show --issue <n>` reads it.

- `pass`: where the stage's `on.pass` says: a stage, `land` or `done`
- `reject`: back to the stage `on.reject` names: always an earlier one
- `blocked`: parked; the same stage runs again when its blockers close
- `already-satisfied`: the workflow ends, with nothing landed
- `escalate`: to the stage's consult (below), or a human where it says so

Only `pass` and `reject` are keys of `on`: the other three mean the same at every stage. `done` ends the workflow with nothing to land; `land` hands the issue's PR to the landing (below). A stage with no `reject` may not declare one. Following `pass` alone from any stage must come to `land` or `done`, and every stage must be reached from the first: a loop back is made with `reject` only.

A stage may split its issue: open issues, take each in, then declare `blocked` on them. When they close, it judges the whole. The team file's `split` key may be false to omit this procedure from briefs ([`afkconvoy help team`](help:team)); true is the default.

A stage that may commit and finds its gate red for a defect outside its issue — what the gate merged in is red the same way gated alone — opens that defect's issue itself, unless an open one already records it, takes it in the same way, and declares `blocked` on it. When it closes, the stage runs again and gates again. The train worker does the same for a base branch that is red without the train: it takes the defect's issue in with `afkconvoy intake --train`, to the team's first workflow unless another fits it clearly better, and has no issue to park.

## Rework and its breakers

Rework is a stage running again because a later stage rejected its work or a consult ruled on it. It is counted per issue from the stage records, from where a human last ruled on the issue or sent it to a stage. Two breakers bound it:

- `max_rework`: the rework of one issue, in total
- `max_consecutive_rework`: the rejections in a row by one stage

A count never passes its breaker: the rework that would is not started, and the issue is handed on (below), naming the breaker and every rework's stage and reason. `afkconvoy rehearse` shows which verdict trips one, with no worker started.

## A consult

A stage's consult is asked before a human is: whatever would hand the issue to a human there — its `escalate`, a tripped breaker, a failure, a workflow changed under it — starts it where that human would stand, free to run what they would ([`afkconvoy help humans`](help:humans)). `escalate: { to, do }` names a more senior role, run within its range ([`afkconvoy help roster`](help:roster)); where a stage names none, the stock consult, afkconvoy's own, is asked on what the host kit names for it — its one instruction is to decide as the human would. `{ to: human }` names none: a human, straight. A consult rules (`afkconvoy rule`: the stage runs again; on an `escalate` that is one more rework in total), sends, closes, parks or lets it through. Close and park add no rework ([`afkconvoy help humans`](help:humans) says how to bring a park back). The same hand-off again goes to a human. A consult writes no code.

## A stage `by: human`

No human stands in a workflow unless it names one. A stage `by: human` has no `do`; it starts no worker and holds no claim. The issue waits there until a human declares the stage's verdict with `afkconvoy verdict`.

Anywhere else a human is reached by an escalation: what a consult let through, or what a stage with `to: human` hands on. The human answers with `afkconvoy rule` — the stage runs again under the ruling — or `afkconvoy send`, to a stage of their choosing.

## A landing

A workflow in which a pass leads to `land` names who lands: `land: { by, do }`. The tick after that `pass` starts a new worker in the role `by`, with the skill `do`, within its role's range. It runs the gate on the issue's PR and joins it to the landing train (`afkconvoy land --help`), which lands it on the base branch as it lands any PR. A `land:` no pass leads to is a fault, and so is a `pass: land` with no `land:`.

### `afkconvoy help patrols`

A patrol is a role run on a schedule rather than for an issue: it looks for work, opens issues and takes them in. Read this to add a patrol to a team, to have a repo run one, or to learn how work reaches the fleet with no human labelling it — and how a fleet lock stops everything but one fix.

## What a patrol is, and is not

It is a worker in one role, with one skill, started when its interval has passed, in a checkout of the base branch that is linked to no issue. What it finds — an issue no workflow has taken, a broken base branch, something worth proposing — it writes down as issues, and takes in the ones the fleet is to work.

It is no stage: it owns no issue, belongs to no workflow and declares no verdict. It writes no code: a run that left a commit or opened a PR has failed. And it is no timer for anything else: nothing but a role's skill can be run by one.

## A patrol's file

`patrols/<name>.md` in the team's directory is the patrol `<name>` — words of lowercase letters and digits, each starting with a letter, joined by `-`, 40 characters at most. Of the file only the first `` ```yaml `` block is read:

```yaml
by: <role>
do: <skill>
every: 6h                          # required: a whole number from 1, then m, h or d
max_open: 5                        # required
max_runs_a_day: 4                  # optional: a whole number from 1
max_landed_a_day: 5                # optional: a whole number from 1
```

`by` is a short name of the team file and `do` a skill of that role. `every` is how long after its last run a patrol is due: it is due or it is not, and one that missed ten intervals runs once. Its worker runs its role's range's first ([`afkconvoy help roster`](help:roster)). `max_open` bounds what a patrol gives the fleet: it is not run while that many issues it opened are open.

`max_runs_a_day` bounds how often it runs besides `every`: a patrol whose runs that started in the last 24 hours — rolling, the same on every host — have reached it is not due, whatever `every` says, until the oldest of them is 24 hours old. Each run's record on the remote carries the starts of the day before it; nothing is kept beside it. Left out, it adds no bound. `afkconvoy check` refuses one that bounds nothing: `every: 1h` lets a patrol run at most 24 times a day, so `max_runs_a_day` is at most 23 there, and a patrol run every day or less often has no use for it.

`max_landed_a_day` bounds the issues it opened that GitHub closed as completed in the last 24 hours, rolling and the same on every host. At the bound the patrol waits until enough completions are 24 hours old to leave fewer than the bound. Issues closed as not planned, reopened issues, and issues opened by humans or other patrols do not count. Ownership comes from the latest intake record, regardless of the issue's labels now. Left out, nothing changes. `check` refuses zero, negative, fractional and nonnumeric values. Unlike runs, completions have no daily ceiling from `every` or `max_open`: any positive whole number can bound them. This limits starting runs; a run already going may open more issues. `plan` reports `standing: landed`, `max_landed_a_day`, `landed_in_day` and `until` while it is this bound that holds the patrol back.

## Which patrols a repo runs

The ones its config names, under `patrols` (`afkconvoy config --help`): a team's patrol runs in no repo that does not name it, and a name the team has no patrol for is a fault of `afkconvoy check`. Of several hosts one runs it: the tick that finds a patrol due claims the run on the remote.

## A run

A run takes one slot of `concurrency` until its worker declares it over with `afkconvoy over`, the last line of its brief; a worker that never does is ended once it is gone or has stopped for a grace period. The tick that ends a run closes its terminal and removes its checkout. `afkconvoy plan` says how each patrol stands, and `afkconvoy tick --help` what a tick does about one.

A run that failed keeps its checkout, and the fleet opens an issue with the team's escalate label that says so. The patrol is not run again until a human closes it.

## A run now

A human who wants a patrol's run now — not when its interval has passed — runs `afkconvoy patrol-now <name>` in a checkout of the repo: the next tick runs it, and the command wakes this host's `run` so that tick starts at once. No file changes. The run passes `every` and `max_runs_a_day`, and nothing else: a fleet lock, `max_open` or `max_landed_a_day` reached, a failed run still reported, or a run still going refuse the ask. It is claimed as a due run is, so of several hosts one runs it. It is recorded as the patrol's run, asked for: `every` counts from its start, and `max_runs_a_day` counts it among the day's. What trips you up: `afkconvoy patrol-now --help`.

## Intake

Intake is putting a flow label on an issue: from then on the issue is the fleet's to work, at the first stage of that workflow. A human does it on GitHub, outside any limit. A worker — a patrol's, or a stage's that splits its issue — does it with `afkconvoy intake`, which records who did; the guard refuses a worker the label itself. To choose a workflow a patrol reads what each is for: `afkconvoy flows`.

Two limits hold what workers take in. The repo's `intake_limit` bounds the open issues taken in by any worker, and `afkconvoy intake` refuses past it. A patrol's `max_open` bounds the ones it opened, and refuses nothing: the patrol is not run.

## The fleet lock

A fault every issue shares — the base branch is broken, so every gate is red whatever its PR holds — is not one issue's to escalate. A patrol that finds it, or a stage, opens an issue for the fix and raises the lock on it with `afkconvoy lock`: an open issue carrying the repo's lock label is a fleet lock, in a bound repo or an unbound one.

While one stands the fleet works lock issues only: nothing else is dispatched, no patrol runs, no PR of another issue joins the landing train, and workers already running are left alone. The lock issue is worked as any issue is: in a bound repo it needs a flow label too. Closing the last lock issue ends the lock; a stage that declared `escalate` or stayed silent before it closed then runs again, which is no rework. What trips you up: `afkconvoy lock --help`.

### `afkconvoy help example`

The binary holds one team whole, and writes it where you say:

```sh
afkconvoy scaffold team hospital --example hospital --repo <owner/repo>
afkconvoy check --team <owner/repo>
```

It is the team this project demonstrates itself with, as one repo holds a team: the team at the root, each role under `roles/`. Read it before you design your own, or start from it. Every file written is named below — each as an item of a list, a role's under its directory — with the decision it holds and the rule of afkconvoy's it shows.

## What the team is for

It is modelled on the one Cockroach Labs describes in "An experiment in running a hospital for code". An issue is a patient: routed, worked up into a plan, the plan reviewed, treated under it, the code reviewed, its record audited, and discharged — its PR joins the landing train. Each is a stage a new worker performs in one role: none reviews what it wrote, and none writes code before the plan passed. The Chief is a human: an issue reaches the Chief by escalating, and a consult is asked first.

## The team

- `team.md`: Names the seven roles, each as `./roles/<name>`: a path from the root of the team's own repo, so that the team names no repo and is pushed, forked or renamed with no edit. Its `precedents` has the fleet start a worker in the role `safety` for each ruling a human gives, to propose it as a precedent: none is asked twice.
- `CLAUDE.md`: The team rules: three, given to every worker whatever its role. They say how this team works, and nothing of one codebase or of one role.
- `precedents.md`: Two precedents a human accepted, each saying when it applies. The first is about the demonstration's own code: take it out when the team works yours.

## The workflows

The prose above each yaml block says what its workflow is for: `afkconvoy flows` answers with it, and the role `triage-nurse` routes by it.

- `workflows/fix.md`: Five stages, then the landing.
  - A reviewer that writes nothing: `plan-review` and `code-review` are marked `writes: false`, as `workup` and `discharge` are, and the guard refuses their workers a commit and a push.
  - A role on another harness: the roster lets the attending run pi first, on pi's own name for its model, so `plan-review` has the plan reviewed by something other than what wrote it; the caster puts its code reviews on Claude Code.
  - A stage with a consult: `workup` and `treatment` carry `escalate: { to: attending, do: consult }`. Their `escalate` goes first to a worker in that role, which lets through to a human only what nobody decided.
  - Rework and its breakers: a `reject` leads back to an earlier stage, and past `max_rework: 3` or `max_consecutive_rework: 2` the issue escalates.
  - `land: { by: discharge-nurse, do: land }`: the join is made in the role that audited the record, not by the worker that wrote the code.
- `workflows/chore.md`: Two stages, then the landing: the fewest of any that lands, so it is where the patrol `rounds` takes in the fix of a broken base branch.
- `workflows/design.md`: A workflow that ends with a human: `proposal`, then `sign-off`, a stage `by: human` whose `pass` leads to `done`. Nothing lands. No human stands in a workflow unless its file says so: here the fleet waits for `afkconvoy rule`.

## The patrols

Each names a role, a skill, how often it runs and `max_open`; a repo's config says which of them it runs.

- `patrols/triage.md`: Every ten minutes: takes each open issue that is in no workflow in to the one that fits. It is how an issue opened with no flow label is worked at all.
- `patrols/rounds.md`: A patrol that locks the fleet. Every half hour it runs the gate on the base branch; red twice, it opens an issue, takes it in to `chore` and raises a fleet lock on it. `max_open: 1` is one lock at a time.
- `patrols/research.md`, `patrols/safety-review.md`: Daily, work proposed with its evidence; weekly, the stage records of what went badly, read for what would have caught it a stage earlier. Each opens issues.

## The roles

Each holds its rules, its skills — every `do` above names one — and its limits for claude-code, `.claude/settings.json`. [`afkconvoy help roles`](help:roles) says what goes where.

- `roles/fellow/`: `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/skills/diagnose/SKILL.md`, `.claude/skills/treat/SKILL.md`, `.claude/settings.json`, `.claude/hooks/refuse.sh`, `.claude/hooks/skills-loaded.sh`, `skills-lock.json`
  Works an issue up and treats it. Two hooks, written executable: `refuse.sh` refuses what its rules say a fellow never does — `--no-verify`, a forced push, `git rebase` — and `skills-loaded.sh` a `pass` or a `reject` declared before the skills its skill says to load were loaded in the session.
- `roles/attending/`: `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/skills/review-plan/SKILL.md`, `.claude/skills/review-code/SKILL.md`, `.claude/skills/consult/SKILL.md`, `.claude/settings.json`, `.claude/hooks/refuse.sh`, `.claude/hooks/skills-loaded.sh`, `.pi/extensions/limits.ts`, `skills-lock.json`
  Reviews, and is the consult. A `reject` needs a blocking finding, which keeps rework from the breaker over a name. `refuse.sh` refuses a commit and a push in every stage: the role writes no code, whatever a workflow left unmarked. `limits.ts` is both hooks again, as a pi extension: pi runs no hook of `.claude/settings.json`, so a limit held under two harnesses is written twice. Under pi a skill is loaded by reading its `SKILL.md`, which is what it counts. Without it `check` refuses `plan-review`: its role would hold no limits there.
- `roles/discharge-nurse/`: `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/skills/audit/SKILL.md`, `.claude/skills/land/SKILL.md`, `.claude/settings.json`
  The last check, and the landing role. `audit` is a checklist of the record, not a second look at the code; `land` says only how a conflict is resolved.
- `roles/safety/`: `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/skills/record-precedent/SKILL.md`, `.claude/skills/review/SKILL.md`, `.claude/settings.json`
  `record-precedent` is asked by the team file, `review` by a patrol.
- `roles/triage-nurse/`: `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/skills/triage/SKILL.md`, `.claude/settings.json`
- `roles/infection-control/`: `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/skills/rounds/SKILL.md`, `.claude/settings.json`
- `roles/research/`: `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/skills/propose/SKILL.md`, `.claude/settings.json`

The three that only patrol. The guard refuses a patrol's worker a commit and a push, so their `settings.json` holds no hook, as those of the two above do.
